items.title: Small business survival rates are lower than commonly thought
items.claim: ONS UK Business Demography statistics consistently show what 5-year survival rate for new UK businesses?

options.text: Around 40% — roughly six in ten new UK businesses don't survive five years

items.reveal_title: Most new businesses don't make it
items.reveal:
ONS Business Demography data: of UK enterprises born in 2017, 39.6% survived to 2022. Year-1 survival is around 90%; the attrition is concentrated in years 2-5. SME failure causes (UK Federation of Small Businesses surveys) cluster around cash flow, late payment, and lack of management capacity.

Entrepreneurship narratives in business teaching focus on success stories. The base rate is more sobering and is one reason support programmes (start-up loans, mentoring) emphasise survival skills over growth.
items.why: Survivor bias in business case studies hides the failure rate. A textbook with only successful firms gives a misleading picture of what running a business actually involves.

items.title: Just-in-time becomes a vulnerability under shock
items.claim: Toyota pioneered just-in-time inventory. What happened to Toyota production during the 2011 Tohoku earthquake?

options.text: Toyota's global production fell by around 800,000 vehicles because a single supplier of microcontrollers (Renesas) was damaged

items.reveal:
Renesas's Naka factory in Ibaraki produced ~30% of automotive microcontrollers globally. After the 11 March 2011 earthquake, Toyota's worldwide output dropped sharply through to mid-2011. After Tohoku, Toyota mandated suppliers to map upstream dependencies and hold buffer stocks for critical components — partially abandoning pure JIT.

The 2020-22 COVID semiconductor shortages repeated the lesson industry-wide.
items.why: Lean optimises against ordinary variation. It does not optimise against catastrophic disruption — and the same firms that pioneered it have had to add 'just-in-case' buffers.

items.title: Maximising capacity utilisation isn't always optimal
items.claim: A factory runs at 95% capacity utilisation. Which statement is most accurate?

options.text: This is always the optimal level
Running close to maximum capacity leaves no slack for demand surges, breakdowns or staff absence and tends to raise unit costs through overtime and quality problems
Capacity utilisation has no link to unit cost
Unit costs fall continuously with utilisation

items.reveal:
Hospitals running at >90% bed occupancy have measurably worse patient outcomes (NHS England analyses through the 2010s). Airlines running above 85% load factor face cascading delay risk. Manufacturing plants above 90% have higher defect rates and overtime costs.

Operations researchers use Kingman's formula: waiting time grows non-linearly as utilisation approaches 100%. The textbook assumption that high utilisation is good ignores queueing dynamics.
items.why: Headline utilisation numbers hide trade-offs. The optimal level depends on demand variability, not just on fixed-cost recovery.
